summary.text: Writing valuations as sums over prime powers gives the numerator valuation as \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor^2\) and the denominator valuation as \(\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{r\le \lfloor N/p^i\rfloor} r\lfloor\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor/r\rfloor\), using the valuation of a gcd and the factorial valuation formula; the inequality \(\sum_{r\le m}r\lfloor m/r\rfloor\le m^2\) also establishes exact divisibility. For \(N=np+k\) with \(k<p\), every \(\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor\) for \(i\ge1\) equals \(\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\), so both valuations, and hence their difference giving the quotient’s valuation, are unchanged.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 U_N=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\prod_{r=1}^{N}\gcd(j,r),
 \qquad
 V_N=\prod_{s=1}^{N}\left(\left\lfloor\frac Ns\right\rfloor !\right)^s.
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
 a(N)=\frac{U_N}{V_N}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and obtain formulas for its prime-adic valuations. All products involved are positive, so their prime-adic valuations are well-defined.

For a prime \(q\), write \(\nu_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in a positive integer \(x\). We use the elementary facts
\[
 \nu_q(xy)=\nu_q(x)+\nu_q(y),\qquad
 \nu_q(x^e)=e\nu_q(x),
\]
and
\[
 \nu_q(\gcd(x,y))=\min\bigl(\nu_q(x),\nu_q(y)\bigr).
\]
Also, for positive \(x,y\),
\[
 \min(\nu_q(x),\nu_q(y))
 =\sum_{i\geq 1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid x\,\text{ and }\,q^i\mid y}.
\]
Indeed, the indicator on the right is one precisely for
\(i=1,\ldots,\min(\nu_q(x),\nu_q(y))\), and is zero thereafter.
All sums over \(i\geq1\) below are actually finite.

We first calculate the valuation of the numerator. Additivity over products and the preceding identity give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_q(U_N)
 &=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sum_{r=1}^{N}
      \min\bigl(\nu_q(j),\nu_q(r)\bigr)\\
 &=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sum_{r=1}^{N}\sum_{i\geq1}
      {\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j\,\text{ and }\,q^i\mid r}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Interchanging these finite sums, for each fixed \(i\) there are exactly
\(\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(q^i\) in \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\). Hence there are
\(\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor^2\) ordered pairs \((j,r)\) for which both entries are divisible by \(q^i\). Therefore
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \nu_q(U_N)=\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.}
 \tag{1}
\]

Next we calculate the valuation of the denominator. For every nonnegative integer \(M\), Legendre's formula says
\[
 \nu_q(M!)=\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{M}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
 \tag{2}
\]
For completeness, this follows by writing
\(\nu_q(M!)=\sum_{t=1}^{M}\nu_q(t)\), replacing each \(\nu_q(t)\) by
\(\sum_{i\geq1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid t}\), and observing that there are
\(\lfloor M/q^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(q^i\) from \(1\) to \(M\).

Using (2), additivity of valuations, and the elementary nested-floor identity
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/s\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N}{s q^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_q(V_N)
 &=\sum_{s=1}^{N}s\,\nu_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac Ns\right\rfloor!\right)\\
 &=\sum_{s=1}^{N}s\sum_{i\geq1}
       \left\lfloor\frac{N}{s q^i}\right\rfloor\\
 &=\sum_{i\geq1}\sum_{s=1}^{N}s
       \left\lfloor\frac{N}{s q^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \nu_q(V_N)=\sum_{i\geq1}\sum_{s=1}^{N}s
       \left\lfloor\frac{N}{s q^i}\right\rfloor.}
 \tag{3}
\]

It is useful to rewrite each inner sum in (3). Put
\[
 m_i=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Integer division can be performed successively, and multiplication of the two divisors may be taken in either order, so
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N}{s q^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor}{s}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m_i}{s}\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(s>m_i\), this last floor is zero. Consequently
\[
 \sum_{s=1}^{N}s\left\lfloor\frac{N}{s q^i}\right\rfloor
 =\sum_{s=1}^{m_i}s\left\lfloor\frac{m_i}{s}\right\rfloor.
 \tag{4}
\]
Define
\[
 H(m)=\sum_{s=1}^{m}s\left\lfloor\frac ms\right\rfloor,
 \qquad H(0)=0.
\]
Then (3) and (4) give the especially convenient formula
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \nu_q(V_N)=\sum_{i\geq1}H\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor\right).}
 \tag{5}
\]

We now prove that \(V_N\mid U_N\), so that the ratio defining \(a(N)\) is exact. For each \(m\geq0\) and each \(1\leq s\leq m\),
\[
 s\left\lfloor\frac ms\right\rfloor\leq m.
\]
There are \(m\) summands in \(H(m)\), and hence
\[
 H(m)\leq m^2.
 \tag{6}
\]
Applying (6) with \(m=\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor\), and then summing over \(i\), formulas (1) and (5) show that for every prime \(q\),
\[
 \nu_q(V_N)
 \leq \sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2
 =\nu_q(U_N).
\]
By unique prime factorization, one positive integer divides another exactly when its valuation at every prime is no larger. Therefore
\[
 V_N\mid U_N.
 \tag{7}
\]
In particular, \(a(N)=U_N/V_N\) is a positive integer, and (7) gives
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \nu_q(a(N))=\nu_q(U_N)-\nu_q(V_N).}
 \tag{8}
\]

We now prove the asserted block constancy. Let \(n\) be a positive integer, let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy
\[
 0\leq k<p.
\]
Set
\[
 N_0=np,
 \qquad
 N_1=np+k.
\]
The key observation is that for every integer \(i\geq1\),
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \left\lfloor\frac{N_1}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor.}
 \tag{9}
\]
To see this, first divide by \(p\). Since \(0\leq k<p\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
For \(i\geq1\), division by \(p^i=p\,p^{i-1}\) can be done by first dividing by \(p\) and then by \(p^{i-1}\). Thus both sides of (9) equal
\(\lfloor n/p^{i-1}\rfloor\).

Apply formula (1) with \(q=p\). By (9), every summand in the valuation of \(U_{N_0}\) equals the corresponding summand in the valuation of \(U_{N_1}\). Hence
\[
 \nu_p(U_{np})=\nu_p(U_{np+k}).
 \tag{10}
\]

Likewise, formula (5) shows that the denominator valuation depends on \(N\) only through the collection of integers
\(\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor\):
\[
 \nu_p(V_N)=\sum_{i\geq1}H\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right).
\]
Again (9) makes the terms for \(N_0=np\) and \(N_1=np+k\) equal one by one, so
\[
 \nu_p(V_{np})=\nu_p(V_{np+k}).
 \tag{11}
\]

Finally, subtract (11) from (10), using (8) at \(N=np\) and at \(N=np+k\). This gives
\[
 \nu_p(a(np))=\nu_p(a(np+k))
 \qquad(0\leq k<p).
\]
As \(k\) ranges from \(0\) through \(p-1\), this is precisely
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
 =\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))
 =\cdots
 =\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
which proves the conjecture.
